title: Spectroscopy
description: Read IR, UV–visible, and proton NMR evidence together.
objectives: Relate conjugation, photon energy, and absorbance
Interpret NMR shifts, integrals, and splitting

sources.label: Supplied Kaplan curriculum: Chapter 11; section scope checked against local body and summary

cards.rule: IR probes molecular vibrations. A vibration absorbs IR when it changes the molecular dipole moment. Useful approximate regions: alcohol O–H 3200–3600 cm⁻¹ (often broad); acid O–H 2500–3300 (very broad); C=O about 1650–1800; nitrile about 2210–2260. N–H is often near 3300, generally less broad than hydrogen-bonded OH.
cards.cue: Use a band pattern, not one magic number. The fingerprint region below about 1500 cm⁻¹ helps comparison.
cards.trap: Carbonyl positions vary with functional group, conjugation, ring strain, and environment. Absence of an OH band may support a structure, but sample conditions matter. IR alone seldom gives complete connectivity.
cards.app: Follow loss of a carbonyl band and appearance of OH when monitoring a carbonyl reduction, together with other evidence.

steps.label: 1. Carbonyl signature
steps.text: A simple saturated acyclic ketone often absorbs near 1715 cm⁻¹. The illustrative plot marks a band position, not an experimentally measured spectrum.

diagram.caption: Schematic ketone absorption; not measured data. Real IR spectra often plot transmittance downward.

steps.label: 2. Compare OH
steps.text: An alcohol has an O–H vibration often broadened by hydrogen bonding. Converting acetone to propan-2-ol changes both the C=O and O–H evidence.

diagram.caption: Schematic hydrogen-bonded alcohol: broad OH and no ketone carbonyl. Widths and intensities are illustrative.

steps.label: 3. Acid pattern
steps.text: A carboxylic acid can show both a carbonyl band and a very broad OH band extending across roughly 2500–3300 cm⁻¹. Interpret them together.

diagram.caption: Schematic carboxylic acid: very broad OH together with C=O; not measured data.

lessons.label: UV–visible: conjugation and energy
lessons.title: UV–visible: conjugation and energy
lessons.tag: Longer wavelength means lower photon energy

cards.rule: UV–visible absorption promotes electrons between electronic states. In many comparable conjugated pi systems, increasing conjugation lowers the transition energy and shifts absorption to longer wavelength. Photon energy obeys E=hc/λ. Beer–Lambert law is A=εlc in its linear regime. For a simple pi system, a pi → pi* excitation can promote an electron from the highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO) to the lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO). Extended conjugation often narrows that gap in comparable systems; allowed transitions and actual spectra also depend on the molecule.
cards.cue: More extended conjugation often gives a red shift. Doubling wavelength halves photon energy.
cards.trap: Conjugation trends compare appropriate related systems, not every possible molecule. UV absorption does not uniquely identify a structure. Beer–Lambert requires compatible units and an appropriate concentration range.
cards.app: Conjugated chromophores underlie retinal photochemistry and many biological absorbance measurements.

steps.label: 1. Follow conjugation
steps.text: Alternating C=C–C=C bonds create a connected p-orbital system. Adjacent p orbitals must remain sufficiently aligned for conjugation.

steps.label: 2. Connect wavelength to energy
steps.text: Relative to an isolated comparable alkene, conjugation often reduces the pi-to-pi-star transition energy. Use E=hc/λ to translate that smaller gap into longer wavelength.

rule.title: Longer wavelength means lower photon energy

cards.rule: Chemical shift reports environment; integration reports relative proton count; splitting reports coupling. In simple first-order cases, coupling to n equivalent neighboring protons produces n+1 lines. Equivalent protons do not split one another. Deshielded protons appear downfield at higher ppm.
cards.cue: Shift = neighborhood; area = population; splitting = neighbors. Upfield means lower ppm and greater shielding; downfield means higher ppm. Tetramethylsilane (TMS) is commonly assigned δ = 0 ppm. Coupling constant J is the line spacing in Hz, not the integral or chemical shift.
cards.trap: n+1 is a limited first-order rule, not universal. Nonequivalent neighbors can give more complex patterns; exchangeable OH/NH protons often do not show the expected simple coupling. Chemical equivalence depends on symmetry and timescale. NMR requires nonzero nuclear spin. Odd-mass isotopes such as ¹H and ¹³C are active; odd-atomic-number nuclei with even mass, such as ²H and ¹⁴N, can also be active. Even-proton/even-neutron nuclei such as ¹²C and ¹⁶O have spin zero. Some active isotopes have broad or difficult signals, so activity alone does not guarantee easy detection.
cards.app: Typical rough proton regions: alkyl 0–3 ppm; C next to O often 3–4.5; vinylic about 4.5–6.5; aromatic 6–8.5; aldehydic 9–10; acid OH often 10–13. Use the full pattern.

steps.label: 1. Three proton sets
steps.text: Ethyl ethanoate has acyl methyl, OCH2, and terminal ethyl methyl proton sets. Their integrals are 3:2:3. The carbonyl carbon has no H. The three green carbon sites carry separate proton environments, not one combined set. Their positions and integrals distinguish them; the orange carbonyl carbon carries no H.

diagram.caption: Schematic proton NMR: Signal 1 near 4.1 ppm (2H), Signal 2 near 2.0 (3H), Signal 3 near 1.2 (3H). Signal numbers are not atom letters; cluster spacing is illustrative, not a measured J.

steps.label: 2. Ethyl splitting
steps.text: OCH2 couples to three neighboring methyl H atoms, giving a quartet in a simple first-order picture. The terminal CH3 couples to two methylene H atoms, giving a triplet.

diagram.caption: Schematic proton NMR: Signal 1 near 4.1 ppm (2H), Signal 2 near 2.0 (3H), Signal 3 near 1.2 (3H). Signal numbers are not atom letters; cluster spacing is illustrative, not a measured J.

steps.label: 3. Acyl methyl
steps.text: The acyl methyl has no H-bearing carbon immediately across the carbonyl bond, so it is approximately a singlet in this example. Do not apply n+1 by counting every H anywhere in the molecule.

diagram.caption: Schematic proton NMR: Signal 1 near 4.1 ppm (2H), Signal 2 near 2.0 (3H), Signal 3 near 1.2 (3H). Signal numbers are not atom letters; cluster spacing is illustrative, not a measured J.

cards.rule: For ordinary neutral closed-shell organic formulas, degree of unsaturation (DBE) = (2C+2+N−H−X)/2; O and divalent S do not enter. A ring or double bond contributes one DBE; a triple bond contributes two. Then combine IR group evidence with NMR environments and integrations.
cards.cue: Formula constrains possibilities; IR finds groups; NMR organizes the skeleton.
cards.trap: A single NMR signal can represent several equivalent groups. DBE says how much unsaturation exists, not where it is. Do not force phosphorus-rich or unusual-valence formulas into this simple equation.
cards.app: Passage-based structure identification rewards eliminating structures inconsistent with even one reliable observation.

steps.label: 1. Formula constraint
steps.text: C3H6O has DBE=(2×3+2−6)/2=1. A carbonyl can account for that entire unit of unsaturation.

steps.label: 2. Add two measurements
steps.text: Suppose IR shows a ketone-like C=O band and proton NMR shows a single 6H singlet near 2 ppm. Two symmetry-equivalent methyl groups adjacent to C=O fit those data.

steps.label: 3. Challenge an alternative
steps.text: Propanal shares C3H6O and DBE=1 with acetone, and both have C=O absorption. But propanal has an aldehydic H (shown explicitly as CH at the terminal carbonyl carbon) and multiple proton environments; it does not fit the single 6H singlet. Compare every observation, not just formula and IR.
